title: The Honjo Masamune
subtitle: Mejiro, Tokyo · 1945–46
voice_instructions: Measured, quiet, a little hushed — calm and unhurried, but with a touch more forward energy than a long documentary; the cold voice of something that read the whole file. Never sensational. Small pauses.
grade: Muted documentary still, Japan in the post-war winter of 1945 to 1946, polished steel and warm lamp-gold highlights against cold grey-blue shadows, melancholy and uncanny, cinematic vertical composition with one centred subject, fine film grain. Single image, not a collage, no text, no signage, no people, no faces.

beats.vo: One of Japan's most celebrated swords was last seen at a Tokyo police station. Nineteen forty-six.
beats.img: A single long, gently curved Japanese sword blade of polished steel, large and filling the middle third of the frame, held upright and slightly angled on a simple dark wooden sword stand, a faint misty wavy temper line along its edge, the steel gleaming bright silver under one warm lamp, clearly legible at small size, in a bare small 1940s police station room with a cold grey plaster wall softly out of focus behind, no people.

beats.vo: The Honjo Masamune, made by the smith Masamune around thirteen hundred. Named a National Treasure in nineteen thirty-nine.
beats.img: An old Japanese sword in a plain black lacquered scabbard resting on a low two-tier wooden sword stand, centred, inside a dim traditional storehouse with dark timber walls and paper screens, a single shaft of pale gold light falling across the lacquer, plain fittings with no crests or markings, quiet and reverent, no people.

beats.vo: In December nineteen forty-five, under occupation orders, the Tokugawa family handed it in to police, with thirteen others.
beats.img: A row of long swords, each wrapped in plain pale cloth, laid side by side on a bare wooden bench in a small post-war Tokyo police station, centred, cold winter light from a frosted window, a single paper-shaded lamp, worn floorboards, no markings, no people.

beats.vo: In January, police passed the swords to an American soldier recorded as Sergeant Coldy Bimore. No one by that name has ever been identified.
beats.img: A lone 1940s US Army jeep parked, empty, outside a small wooden Japanese police station on a narrow Tokyo street in winter dusk, centred, its headlights on, light snow on the road, one warm window glowing, cold blue shadows, no people, no signage.

beats.vo: Some believe it was destroyed. Some, that it went to America. It has never been found.
beats.img: An empty open wooden sword box lined with faded silk, a long curved sword-shaped hollow still pressed into the lining, centred on a dark table, dim cold light from one side, a little dust, quiet and still, no people.

facts.claim: The Honjo Masamune is a katana attributed to the smith Goro Nyudo Masamune (c. 1264–1343, active roughly 1288–1328), i.e. made around the turn of the fourteenth century

It is one of Japan's most celebrated swords: 'one of the best known of the swords created by Masamune... among the finest Japanese swords ever made'; 'the most famous lost sword in Japanese history'; 'among the greatest lost treasures of the world'
It was designated a National Treasure (Kokuho) in 1939 under the prewar 1929 law (27 May 1939); it is not listed under the postwar 1950 system because its whereabouts have been unknown since 1946
It was held for centuries by the Tokugawa (passed shogun to shogun through the Edo period); last known owner Tokugawa Iemasa (d. 1963)
Under the Allied occupation, swords had to be surrendered (SCAPIN 181, Sept 1945; collection through local police stations)
In December 1945 Tokugawa Iemasa turned in the Honjo Masamune and 13 other heirloom swords (14 in all) to the police station at Mejiro, Tokyo

In January 1946 (receipt dated 18 January 1946) the Mejiro police gave the swords to a man recorded as 'Sgt. Coldy Bimore', usually given as of the Foreign Liquidations Commission of AFWESPAC (one account says 7th Cavalry, so the unit is left out of the film); the name may be a garbled phonetic spelling

No soldier by that name has ever been identified ('No serviceman by that name has ever been identified'; 'there was no Sgt. Coldy Bimore working for AFWESPAC'; 'no one named Coldy Bimore in that regiment'; 'Neither the sergeant nor the sword has been identified or located since')
'Last seen at a Tokyo police station, 1946': the last documented custody is the Mejiro police handover in January 1946; no credible sighting since
Theories (unproven): destroyed with the mass of confiscated swords (melted/dumped); or taken to the United States and held privately

Still not found as of 2026: Boing Boing (June 2026) 'nobody knows where it is'; EsoVitae (May 2026) no credible sighting since 1946; Toukenza (April 2026) location remains unknown as of 2026; Japanese Wikipedia '1945年、連合軍に接収され、以後所在不明'. The 2014 Masamune news concerned a different blade (Shimazu Masamune)
